purpose: Betamethasone is used to reduce swelling, redness, and irritation caused by many different conditions including skin problems, allergies, arthritis, and inflammatory diseases. It can be applied to the skin as a cream or ointment, given as a shot, or taken by mouth depending on what your doctor is treating. Pregnant women sometimes receive betamethasone injections to help speed up their baby's lung development if early delivery is expected.
how_it_works: Betamethasone works by calming down your immune system and reducing inflammation in your body. Think of inflammation as your body's alarm system going off too strongly — this medication helps turn down that alarm. It blocks the chemicals in your body that cause swelling, redness, pain, and irritation.
common_side_effects: When used on the skin: thinning of the skin, stretch marks, skin irritation, or changes in skin color. When taken as a shot or by mouth: increased appetite, weight gain, trouble sleeping, mood changes, increased blood sugar, and upset stomach. Long-term use can cause more serious effects like weakened bones or a puffy face.
warnings: Do not stop taking this medication suddenly if you have been using it for a long time — your doctor will help you slowly reduce the dose. Tell your doctor if you have diabetes, high blood pressure, osteoporosis, or any infections, as this medication can make infections harder to fight. Avoid contact with people who have chickenpox or measles while taking this medication. Do not use more than directed on the skin, especially on the face or in children.
typical_dosing: Dosing depends on what condition is being treated and the form of the medication. Skin creams or ointments are usually applied once or twice a day to the affected area in a thin layer. Injections are given by a healthcare professional and the dose varies widely. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — never change your dose without asking your doctor first.
